summary.text: Polynomial long division is a step-by-step method for dividing one polynomial by another to get a quotient and a remainder.
The remainder is zero exactly when the divisor is a factor of the dividend, so the method tests for factors and factors them out.
If one root r of a polynomial is known, dividing by (x − r) factors it into (x − r) times a quotient of one lower degree.

facts.label: Zero remainder
facts.value: Remainder 0 happens only when the divisor is a factor

facts.label: Shortcut method
facts.value: Synthetic division needs less writing, especially for linear divisors

facts.label: Field coefficients
facts.value: Coefficients must come from one field, such as the rationals

facts.label: Tangent lines
facts.value: Division by (x − r)² gives the tangent line at x = r

facts.label: Error detection
facts.value: Cyclic redundancy checks use the remainder to catch message errors

items.prompt: A student divides polynomial A by polynomial B and the leftover comes out to exactly 0. What can she conclude?

options.label: A has lower degree than B
B is a factor of A, dividing it evenly
The quotient must also be 0
A and B share no roots

items.explain: A zero remainder happens if and only if the divisor is a factor of the dividend.

items.prompt: A polynomial of degree 5 has one known root r. You divide it by (x − r). What kind of quotient do you get?

options.label: Degree 5, with a nonzero remainder
Degree 4, with a remainder of zero
Degree 3, with a remainder of zero
Degree 6, with a remainder of zero

items.explain: A known root r gives a quotient of degree n − 1, here 4, and since r is a root the remainder must be zero.

items.prompt: How does the long division you learned in school for ordinary numbers relate to the polynomial version?

options.label: The two methods are unrelated tricks
Polynomial division swaps the digits for letters
Both give only whole-number answers
It is the same algorithm with x replaced by 10

items.explain: The arithmetic algorithm is the polynomial one with x replaced by 10, plus the restriction that coefficients be non-negative.

items.prompt: You must divide a polynomial by a monic polynomial of degree 1 and want less writing. Which method fits?

options.label: Synthetic division
Guessing a quotient
Euclid’s tangent trick
Dividing term by term in reverse

items.explain: Synthetic division is an alternative to long division that needs less writing and fewer calculations when the divisor is monic and linear.

items.prompt: A polynomial of degree 1 is divided by one of degree 3 with the long division algorithm. What comes out?

options.label: A quotient of degree 2 and no remainder
An error, because the division is impossible
A quotient of 0 and the original polynomial as remainder
A quotient equal to the original and remainder 0

items.explain: When the numerator’s degree is lower than the denominator’s, the result is just (0, numerator) and the loop is never entered.

items.prompt: You want the tangent line to a polynomial’s graph at one point using division. What divisor do you use?

options.label: The square of the linear factor, (x − r)²
The linear factor alone, (x − r)
The sum of the two roots, (x + r)
The point’s height, r

items.explain: The remainder of dividing P(x) by (x − r)² is the tangent line at x = r, whether or not r is a root.
